answer: The pleasure principle is defined as the law of the good, which is the wohl, or well-being [bien-étre]. In practice, it means that this principle would submit the subject to the same phenomenal succession that determines its objects. This succession is what determines the subject's well-being.

contexts.text: The pleasure principle is the law of the good which is the wohl, let us say well-being [bien-étre]. No phenomenon can claim for itself a constant relation to pleasure. Thus no law of such a good can be enunciated which would define as will the subject who would introduce it into his practice.

answer: The equation of value establishes an inverse relation between the price and the quantity of merchandise obtained. This equation retains in itself the difference in nature between values, which is the necessity of their difference. Therefore, the equation of value is fundamentally linked to the concept of difference in the nature of values.

So much of one equals so much of the other: an inverse relation between the price and the quantity of the merchandise obtained. Now, what is at stake is not at all what is clear, but what it conceals, in terms of what the equation retains in itself, which is the difference in nature between values thus connected and the necessity of their difference.

answer: The symbolic process is what dominates and governs all things in the human world, structuring it through words and language. It is a system that is not accessible to the animal world, implying a complete and precise knowledge of what it means.

contexts.text: I don’t want to begin developing a theory of knowledge here, but it is obvious that the things of the human world are things in a universe structured by words, that language, symbolic processes, dominate and govern all. When we seek to explore the frontier between the animal and the human world, it is apparent to what extent the symbolic process as such doesn’t function in the animal world — a phenomenon that can only be a matter of astonishment for us. A difference in the intelligence, the flexibility, and the complexity of the apparatuses involved cannot be the only means of explaining that absence. That man is caught up in symbolic processes of a kind to which no animal has access cannot be resolved in psychological terms, since it implies that we first have a complete and precise knowledge of what this symbolic process means.

question: What is the symbolic process as such in relation to the human world?
source_text: I don’t want to begin developing a theory of knowledge here, but it is obvious that the things of the human world are things in a universe structured by words, that language, symbolic processes, dominate and govern all. When we seek to explore the frontier between the animal and the human world, it is apparent to what extent the symbolic process as such doesn’t function in the animal world — a phenomenon that can only be a matter of astonishment for us. A difference in the intelligence, the flexibility, and the complexity of the apparatuses involved cannot be the only means of explaining that absence. That man is caught up in symbolic processes of a kind to which no animal has access cannot be resolved in psychological terms, since it implies that we first have a complete and precise knowledge of what this symbolic process means.

answer: The description g’ra delgat e gen signifies that plumpness was an element of the sex appeal during that period. Furthermore, e gen is used to signify graceful. This description is used to characterize the feminine object in this poetic field.

contexts.text: The fact that on occasion her body is described as g’ra delgat e gen — that means that plumpness was part of the sex appeal of the period, e gen signifying graceful — should not deceive you, since she is always described in that way. In this poetic field the feminine object is emptied of all real substance. That is what made it easy subsequently for a metaphysical poet such as Dante, for example, to choose a person whom we definitely know existed — namely, little Beatrice whom he fell for when she was nine years old, and who stayed at the center of his poétry from the Vita Nuova to The Divine Comedy — and to make her the equivalent of philosophy or indeed, in the end, of the science of the sacred. That also enabled him to appeal to her in terms that are all the more sensual because the person in question is close to allegory. It is only when the person involved is transformed into a symbolic function that one is able to speak of her in the crudest terms.

answer: When Freud formulated the term unconscious thought, adding sit venia verbo in his Traumdeutung, he was asserting a specific meaning. He was stating that the thought itself is equivalent to the thing articulated in language. Therefore, the concept of unconscious thought in that context is strictly defined by its relationship to language and articulation.

The fact that this may happen without one’s knowledge might have been described as outlandish for a long time, but for us this isn’t so — the very idea of an unconscious thought, this great practical paradox that Freud gave, means nothing else.
